primitives.name: Sequential Performance Model
primitives.verbatim_quote: 2 + Σ_{m<e} γ_{m,e} Y_{i,j,m} — performance in each event depends linearly on all preceding events in the same decathlon (captures fatigue/similarity).
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'Y_{i,j,e}': 'performance in event e for athlete i at time j (time/distance)', 'α_{i,e}': 'athlete-specific intercept for event e (dimensionless)', 'β_{d,e}': 'coefficient for basis function d in event e (dimensionless)', 'φ_d(age)': 'nonlinear basis function of age (dimensionless)', 'γ_{m,e}': 'dependence coefficient of prior event m on current event e (dimensionless)', 'ε_{i,j,e}': 'error term for event e (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Linear dependence on preceding events, shared age curve basis functions, fixed event order.
primitives.breakdown_regime: At extreme ages or when event order changes, model may fail due to extrapolation.

layer2.mapping: Maps to GSE's state-transition models where each game phase depends on prior phases, incorporating environmental covariates.
layer2.telemetry: RMSE of predicted vs actual event performance under cross-validation.

primitives.name: Age Curve Basis Function
primitives.verbatim_quote: 1 (baseline): total points P_{i,j} = α̃_i + Σ_d β̃_d φ_d(age) + ε — athlete random intercept + nonlinear age basis.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'P_{i,j}': 'total decathlon points for athlete i at time j (points)', 'α̃_i': 'athlete-specific random intercept (points)', 'β̃_d': 'coefficient for basis function d (points)', 'φ_d(age)': 'nonlinear basis function of age (dimensionless)', 'ε': 'error term (points)'}
primitives.assumptions: Nonlinear age trajectory captured by basis functions, shared across athletes except intercepts.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Extrapolation beyond observed age range leads to unreliable predictions.

layer2.mapping: Used in GSE to derive player performance kernels over time, accounting for aging and experience.
layer2.telemetry: Mean squared error between predicted and observed total points over athlete career.

primitives.name: Event Scoring Transformation
primitives.verbatim_quote: - Event order fixed: Day 1 (100m, LJ, SP, HJ, 400m), Day 2 (110mH, DT, PV, JT, 1500m); World Athletics scoring table (Table A2 coefficients a, b, c per event) converts performances to points.
primitives.latex: P_e = \begin{cases} a(b - y)^c & \text{track events} \\ a(y - b)^c & \text{field events} \end{cases}
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'P_e': 'points for event e (points)', 'y': 'performance in event e (time or distance)', 'a, b, c': 'event-specific scoring coefficients (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Fixed scoring system applies uniformly, no environmental modifiers considered.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Performance outside standard ranges may yield undefined or extreme point values.

layer2.mapping: Analogous to GSE’s scoring systems for game phases, where performance metrics translate into outcome values.
layer2.telemetry: Accuracy of predicted points against actual decathlon totals.

The core insight of the paper lies in modeling decathlon performance as a sequence of dependent events, where each event's outcome is influenced by prior performances. This is formalized using a Bayesian hierarchical model with athlete-specific intercepts and shared nonlinear age curves. The model uses cubic splines or polynomials to capture age-related performance dynamics, and includes linear dependence on preceding events to reflect fatigue or skill transfer. The scoring transformation maps raw performance to points using fixed coefficients, enabling total score estimation. The failure mode arises from assuming linearity in inter-event dependencies and lack of environmental data, which limits generalization. The model's strength is its compositional structure, allowing for simulation of hypothetical athlete careers and estimation of maximal achievable scores. In GSI, this translates to probabilistic forecasting of peak human performance. In GSE, it provides a framework for modeling sequential game states with temporal and contextual dependencies.
